saidimusic.window: c. 1700 onward (tree date; no page read dates the start: the Mataqil musician family goes back seven generations; first recordings found 1976)
saidimusic.sound: The folk music of Upper Egypt (the Sa'id, around Luxor), played by hereditary musician clans at weddings and mawlids: the two-string rababa fiddle with darbuka and duff behind folk songs, mawwal and the Hilali epic, and the mizmar sa'idi shawm band with the double-headed tabl baladi that drives the tahtib stick dance.
markers: A piercing mizmar shawm played with circular breathing, often two or three at once
A booming tabl baladi bass drum beating heavy dum against fast tak strokes
A two-string rababa fiddle trilling around a rough solo voice
fits: Hizzy al-Assaya: Saidi Music from Upper Egypt (album)
near: Cairo working-class pop about city life, sung by a shaabi star with an urban band, not a village rababa or mizmar ensemble
Cairo art song: an hour-long performance with a large orchestra composed by Mohammed Abdel Wahab, not rural Upper Egyptian folk music

lavani.window: Beginnings traced to the 1560s; prominent in the late Peshwa era (poet-singers such as Ram Joshi, 1762–1812, and Honaji Bala); on record through Marathi tamasha films from 1947 and still current (film lavanis of 2010 and 2022).
lavani.sound: Marathi song-and-dance of the tamasha stage: a woman singer, often in a quick tempo, over the powerful rhythm of the dholki drum, singing of love, longing and flirtation. The public stage form is phadachi lavani; the seated, private baithakichi lavani is sung before a small audience, and Honaji Bala brought the tabla in place of the dholki.
markers: A driving dholki drum rhythm under the voice
A woman singer in a quick tempo, teasing and flirtatious
Songs of love and longing for an absent or reluctant lover
fits: Kasa Kay Patil Bara Hay Ka
near: A Hindi film item song by the composers of Natarang's lavanis: the same stage-dance energy, but a Bollywood item number with no page calling it a lavani
A Marathi film dance duet from the same era and singer, filed as folk, filmi, pop and dance: a male-female hit tune, not a woman's lavani over the dholki

maloya.window: 18th century onward (born among the enslaved; banned until 1981; first public performance 1959, on record from 1972)
maloya.sound: Réunion's slave-descended music, sung in Réunion Creole: a solo voice answered by a chorus over a rolling ternary beat from the roulèr barrel drum, the kayamb rattle, piker and sati idiophones and the bobre musical bow; sacred forms in the servis kabaré ancestor rites, secular forms at the kabar, and since the late 1970s also electric versions with guitar, bass and keyboards.
markers: A low roulèr barrel drum, played with both hands, rolling in a ternary pulse
The swish of the kayamb rattle and the struck twang of the bobre musical bow
A solo singer answered by a chorus in Réunion Creole
near: Mauritian séga typique by 'le roi du séga mauricien': the ravanne frame-drum dance song of Mauritius, not Réunion's roulèr-and-kayamb maloya
Réunion séga, the island's other traditional music: a ballroom-descended dance song with European string and wind instruments, where maloya uses only percussion and the bow

rara.sound: Haitian street-procession music of Lent and Easter week, best known from Léogâne: bands of single-note bamboo trumpets (vaksin) play interlocking hocket patterns, tapping the tubes with sticks, over strapped marching drums, tin konet horns, scrapers, maracas and rattles made of recycled metal, while singers lead satirical, double-meaning songs in Haitian Creole; Haitian cane workers carry it into the Dominican Republic as gagá.
markers: Single-note bamboo vaksin trumpets locking together in a looping hocket, tapped with sticks
Marching drums, tin horns, scrapers and rattles heard moving down a road
A crowd chorus singing teasing, double-meaning songs in Haitian Creole
fits: Rara in Haiti / Gaga in the Dominican Republic (album)
Caribbean Revels: Haitian Rara and Dominican Gaga (album)
Alan Lomax in Haiti, Volume 4: Rara: vodou in motion (album)
Rara in Haiti: Street Music of Haiti (album)
near: Electric roots band (guitars, bass, keyboards) drawing on Vodou songs: a stage song, not a marching vaksin band
Uses rara horns and petro drums inside a rock-band arrangement rather than a street procession
A mizik rasin band named after rara, playing arranged band music, not a festival procession recording

huapango.window: Roots in colonial-era son (18th century, Sierra Huasteca); the son huasteco as now played dates from the 19th century, with the violin-jarana-huapanguera trio standard from the 1950s; on record from the 1960s (earliest verified album 1966) to today.
huapango.sound: String-trio music of La Huasteca in northeastern Mexico: a virtuoso, flamboyant violin leads, the deep five-course huapanguera and the small jarana huasteca strum a rhythm that mixes duple and triple metre, and two singers trade improvised and traditional coplas in high voices with falsetto breaks while the violin falls silent and dancers' zapateado softens.
markers: High duet singing with sudden falsetto breaks
Ornate, improvised violin runs between the sung verses
Strummed jarana and deep huapanguera in a lilting rhythm that shifts between 3 and 2 feel
fits: El ave de mi soñar: Mexican Sones Huastecos (album)
El viejo Elpidio y sus huastecos
Music of México, Vol. 3: La Huasteca: Huapangos y Sones Huastecos (album)
near: A huapango sung with mariachi trumpets, violins and guitarrón and a long, showy falsetto, with no trio and no zapateado
A composed huapango-style song (Tomás Méndez, 1954) sung by a ranchera star with mariachi backing, not a traditional son played by a Huastecan trio
Huapango rhythm played as fast norteño dance music on accordion and bajo sexto instead of violin, jarana and huapanguera

verbunkos.window: c. 1760 onward (took shape in the second half of the 18th century, first known printed piece 1784, played at recruiting until conscription in 1848–49; recorded by Hungarian Gypsy bands from the 1950s and kept alive as a village men's dance and in the táncház revival)
verbunkos.sound: Hungarian recruiting-dance music: a proud, slow lassú in sharp dotted rhythm followed by a fast friss of virtuosic running notes, played by Romani bands of violins and cimbalom with ornamented violin figures and augmented-second turns; the ancestor of the csárdás, still danced in villages as the men's verbunk.
markers: A slow, proud lassú in short-long dotted rhythm that breaks into a fast, running friss
Lead violin spinning ornamented runs over a Gypsy band of strings and cimbalom
Augmented-second and diminished-seventh turns in a major or minor melody
near: Béla Bartók, Joseph Szigeti, Benny Goodman

Bartók's 1938 concert trio for clarinet, violin and piano names its first movement after the verbunkos, but it is a composed modernist work, not dance music played by a band; modernism is the right period id rather than romantic or classical
Piano Trio in G major, Hob. XV:25 "Gypsy Rondo": III. Rondo all'Ongarese
Haydn's 1795 finale borrows verbunkos tunes and Gypsy effects for a Viennese piano trio: classical-period art music in the Hungarian manner
Liszt's solo piano rhapsody takes its lassan-friska form from the Hungarian dance, but it is a Romantic concert piece for one virtuoso pianist
Sándor Déki Lakatos and His Gipsy Band

Same Gypsy band and sound, but a medley of composed popular songs (magyar nóta) and a csárdás, not a recruiting dance

morenadaanddiablad.window: c. 1790 onward (scores from the 1860s; first organised diablada troupe 1904; brass-band diablada in Puno from 1962; on record from the 1960s)
morenadaanddiablad.sound: The brass-band dance music of the Oruro Carnival and the Andean fiestas of Bolivia, Peru's Puno and northern Chile. The morenada is a slow, heavy dance march for trumpets, tubas, bass drum and cymbals, with the dancers' matraca rattles grinding over it. The diablada, the devil dance, comes in two parts: a march, then the devil's mecapaqueña. Both were once played on sikus and are now played by bronze bands; Oruro alone has about 150 bands. Andean folk groups also record both as named pieces.
markers: A slow, heavy, swaying march beat on bass drum and cymbals
Massed trumpets, horns and tubas playing the tune together
The rasping crank of matraca rattles over the band
fits: Antología de la Diablada Azoguini Puño - Bodas de Oro (album)
near: Huayno Cacharpari Amigos de la Policía Nacional
The same Puno brass band and album as its diabladas, but labelled a huayno, the highland song-dance, not a devil-dance march
On the same 1970 LP as their morenada La mariposa, but labelled a huayno, the highland song-dance, not a fiesta march

sevillanas.window: c. 1800 onward (seguidillas danced in Seville since the late 16th century, a distinct dance from the 18th; the modern form arose with the Seville Fair in the later 19th century; 78s from the 1920s, the first records by sevillanas groups from 1950, the boom of 1983-1988)
sevillanas.sound: Seville's festive couple dance song: always a set of four sevillanas in triple time, each a seven-line copla (a seguidilla and a refrain) sung over strummed guitar, palmas and often castanets, the music and the dancers stopping together at the close. The rociera kind for the El Rocío pilgrimage adds the pipe and tabor and, with the Rocío choirs, choral harmony; from the 1960s dedicated vocal groups, bass, electric instruments and orchestral arrangements came in. It borrows flamenco's colour but is not a flamenco palo.
markers: Strummed guitar introduction, then a brisk triple-time beat of palmas and castanets
Four short coplas to a set, music and dancers ending together on the last one
Group voices in harmony singing of Seville, Triana, the Feria and the road to El Rocío
near: Bulerías, a flamenco palo sung solo as free cante in Camarón's new-flamenco style, not the fixed four-copla couple dance of the Feria
A rumba: Gitano party music in a duple rumba groove, not triple-time sevillanas
A rumba by one of the leading sevillanas groups, recorded beside their sevillanas but in rumba rhythm
